themes.theme: An attacker-chosen roster size (n) drives O(n) loop trips and O(n^2) Set insertion inside Constraints.fromTags before any size gate can see or refuse it — every sibling entry point in the same module (degreeOf, Graph ctor, validate, ringGreedy, constrainedGreedy) checks n first; fromTags alone does not.
findingSummaries: `Constraints.fromTags` is the only entry point in the core that takes a roster size on faith. `degreeOf` in the same file, the `Graph` constructor, `validate`, `ringGreedy` and `constrainedGreedy` all guard `n` first; `fromTags` runs `for (let i = 0; i < n; i++)` with no validation and inserts one Set key per same-tag pair, so both the loop trip count and the O(n^2) materialization are paid inside the constructor — `validate`'s MAX_CONSTRAINED_N refusal only ever sees the result. This is the documented deferral in lib/CLAUDE.md; re-verified it still reproduces and re-verified the no-caller condition it rests on (grep across app/src and lib/src finds references only in lib/test), so it stays a deferral rather than becoming gating.
themes.remediation: Move the same n-guard every other function in the module already has (`Number.isInteger(n) && n >= 0 && n <= MAX_CONSTRAINED_N`) to the first statement of `fromTags`, throwing before the loop instead of letting `validate` catch the result afterward — this removes the double-loop's ability to run on an unchecked n rather than adding a new counting pass.

themes.theme: A polish-budget gate accepts a call whose own derived iteration count is provably zero, so an admitted call still pays the fixed all-pairs sweep and copy cost to return its input unchanged.
findingSummaries: `checkPolishSize` and `boundedPolishIterations` split one budget: the size gate charges FIXED_POLISH_SWEEPS * n * (n+m) and the iteration count is derived from what's left of `loopBudget`. For n*(n+m) in the band (MAX_POLISH_WORK-64)/4 < n*(n+m) <= MAX_POLISH_WORK/3, the size gate admits and the derived iteration count is exactly 0, so `polish`/`polishConstrained` pay the full fixed sweeps and two graph copies to return their input byte-for-byte. optimizer.props.test.ts:405 pins the zero-iteration collapse as intended; what's unguarded is that the call is still accepted and still charged for it. Not reachable from either public builder today (their admitted n*(n+m) tops out an order of magnitude below the threshold).
themes.remediation: Fold the two checks into one: have `checkPolishSize` refuse whenever `boundedPolishIterations(n, m, requested, fallback) < 1`, using the same budget in its message — this removes the gap between the two gates rather than adding a combined-check abstraction, since the accept path already computes the derived count and only needs to consult it before returning.

themes.theme: The core's only cited open/closed extension seam (fromTags's TagPolicy switch) has no real caller anywhere, so its claimed 'this seam pays' evidence is structural only and untested by any product usage.
findingSummaries: TagPolicy (line 46) is a union of exactly one string literal ("prohibit_same"), and Constraints.fromTags's switch (lines 114-126) has exactly one case plus a default throw. A trial second case ("require_same") required touching only this switch and the union — no file in lib/src or app/ references TagPolicy or calls fromTags outside lib/test/constrained.test.ts. The switch is structurally trivial to extend (real evidence for the CLAUDE.md OCP claim), but fromTags itself has no live caller anywhere in app/, and no product requirement (PROJECT_PLAN.md F7) names a second policy today.
themes.remediation: No code change now; when F7 gives fromTags a real caller, drop today's speculative-extension trial rather than keep validating an unused second branch — re-derive the OCP claim only against whichever policy actually ships, at the same time the n-guard hardening (from the unbounded-work theme) is finally added to fromTags.

themes.theme: Both swap-polish loops (polish() and polishConstrained()) return a mid-search energy-best snapshot rather than the terminal state of their own accepted-swap trajectory, and expose no field marking where the two diverge — a gap the project's own next roadmap item (F11 construction replay) will hit if it traces these loops the obvious way.
findingSummaries: polish.ts's `g` (the live mutating graph) keeps advancing after `best` is last updated, because Metropolis accepts non-improving moves that mutate `g` but never touch `best` — the loop can run thousands more accepted swaps on `g` after the swap that produced the returned `best = g.copy()`. `PolishResult`'s `iters` is the total loop count, not the index at which `best` was captured. `polishConstrained` in constrainedGreedy.ts has the identical shape and its return type carries no run-level metrics at all. A naive F11 trace (record every applied swap, replay start-to-finish) reconstructs the fully-mutated final `g`, which is NOT the graph either function actually returns.
themes.remediation: Before any F11 tracing work begins, cut the loops off at the point they already stop mattering: once `best` is last updated in polish()/polishConstrained(), the remaining accepted-but-not-best swaps are wasted work relative to what's returned — truncate the run (or the future trace) at that index rather than letting the search continue past its own answer, removing the divergence instead of exposing a new field to describe it.

themes.theme: Comments in index.ts overstate uniformity of how degraded or refused input is represented across output fields and options, obscuring real per-field and per-option differences a maintainer needs to know.
findingSummaries: Comment at lines 285-286 falsely claims the `buddies` field is empty when input is refused; it is actually an n-length array of empty arrays, not an empty array.

Comment at lines 370-371 misleadingly claims `polishIters`, `minSeparation`, and `priorWeight` are all handled identically as 'ignored, not fatal', but they are in fact handled by three different mechanisms.
themes.remediation: Delete both blanket 'empty'/'ignored, not fatal' comments and let each field's actual shape speak for itself at its own line (empty edges array; n empty buddy sublists; polishIters falls back to default; minSeparation and priorWeight are dropped) — removing the false generalization is the fix, not writing a longer accurate one to replace it.

gating.theme: a cost gate admits a call that provably cannot do any of the work it is charging for
gating.summary: `checkPolishSize` and `boundedPolishIterations` split one budget: the size gate charges FIXED_POLISH_SWEEPS * n * (n+m) and the iteration count is derived from `loopBudget` — what is left. That correctly stops the two gates summing past MAX_POLISH_WORK, but nothing asks whether anything is left. For n*(n+m) in the band (MAX_POLISH_WORK - 64)/4 < n*(n+m) <= MAX_POLISH_WORK/3, the size gate admits and the derived iteration count is exactly 0, so `polish`/`polishConstrained` pay the full fixed all-pairs sweeps and two graph copies to return their input byte-for-byte. optimizer.props.test.ts:405 pins `boundedPolishIterations(16000, 16000, 20000, 20000) === 0` as the intended collapse, so the zero is deliberate; what is unguarded is that the call is still ACCEPTED and still pays for it. This is public-API-only: I derived that neither builder can reach the band (buildBuddyGraph's admitted set caps n*(n+m) at ~5.2e7 and buildConstrainedBuddyGraph's at 7.5e7, both an order of magnitude below the 2.16e8 threshold), so it is not reachable from an imported file today.
gating.failure: `polish(ring(11000), { maxIters: 20000 })` — n*(n+m) = 2.42e8, fixed sweeps 7.26e8 against a budget of 8.65e8, so `checkPolishSize` admits — runs for 6.68 s and returns `iters: 0` with an edge list identical to its input. `polishConstrained(ring(11000), new Constraints(11000), { iters: 8000 })` is the worse half: 3.37 s, input returned unchanged, and because it returns a bare `Graph` with no iteration count there is nothing in the return value that distinguishes it from a pass that did work — the exact 'silent no-op sold as work' shape polish.ts's own numbered comment 3 treats as a defect. By contrast `polish(ring(9500))` (n*(n+m) = 1.805e8, just below the band) spends a comparable 7.18 s and does get its 1 iteration.
gating.remediation: Make the accept-set answer the whole question in one place: have `checkPolishSize` (or a single combined `checkPolishBudget(n, m, requested, fallback)`) refuse when `boundedPolishIterations(n, m, requested, fallback) < 1`, with a message naming the same budget — 'the fixed sweeps leave nothing for the loop at (n, m)'. That is not a new constant and it cannot refuse anything the loop would have accepted, since by construction the loop would have run zero times. If refusing is judged too strong for a pass documented as best-effort, return before `energy()`/`copy()` instead, so an admitted-but-idle call is O(1) rather than three all-pairs sweeps.
gating.invariant: For all (n, m, requested >= 1): if `checkPolishSize(n, m)` does not throw, then `boundedPolishIterations(n, m, requested, fallback) - calibrationSweeps >= 1`. Equivalently, for every graph and options on which `polish` returns normally, `result.iters >= 1` whenever `maxIters >= 1` — no accepted call performs the O(n*(n+m)) fixed sweeps and then runs zero accept/reject decisions.

gating.theme: Both swap-polish passes return a mid-search energy-best snapshot, not the terminal state of their own accepted-swap trajectory, and nothing in their public result exposes where the two diverge — which is exactly the gap the project's own next roadmap item (F11 construction replay) will hit if it instruments these loops the obvious way
gating.summary: PROJECT_PLAN.md's F11 entry states plainly that replay needs a construction trace and that this is core work, not UI-only, because Graph.edgeList() only returns a canonical sort. I traced what the natural fix looks like: ringGreedy's for(;;) loop (greedy.ts:171-185) and repairDegrees's pass loop (greedy.ts:265-314) each add edges in a genuine causal order that a trace can record cheaply (O(1) per edge, off the O(n²) hot inner loops) and that order IS the graph returned. polish.ts's loop is different in kind: `g` (the live mutating graph, polish.ts:115-150) keeps advancing after `best` is last updated — Metropolis accepts non-improving moves (line 131) that mutate `g` but never touch `best` — so the loop can run thousands of further accepted-and-kept swaps on `g` after the swap that produced the returned `best` (polish.ts:136-140, `best = g.copy()`). The function returns `best`, not `g`. `PolishResult`'s fields are exactly `{ graph, aspl, connected, iters }` (polish.ts:40-45) — `iters` is the total loop count that ran, not the index at which `best` was captured. `polishConstrained` in constrainedGreedy.ts has the identical shape (constrainedGreedy.ts:220-228, `best = g.copy()` on `next.energy < bestEnergy`), and its return type carries no run-level metrics at all (module comment at constrainedGreedy.ts:139-141 explicitly says so). A naive implementation of F11's trace — record every applied (non-reverted) swap in loop order and replay it start-to-finish — reconstructs the fully-mutated final `g`, which is NOT the graph either function actually returns to its caller.
gating.failure: Recording swap trace S (every applied, non-reverted swap in polish's loop, in order) and replaying all of S against the input graph produces a graph edge-set-identical to the loop's final `g`, which for a typical anneal run (Metropolis accepts moves worse than best) differs from PolishResult.graph (the returned `best`). Concretely: with mode:'anneal' and enough iterations after the last improving accept, `S` replayed in full will diverge from `res.graph`'s edge set, while no field of `res` names the prefix length of `S` that does reconstruct it.
gating.remediation: Before instrumenting these loops for F11, add the missing correspondence explicitly rather than reconstructing it after the fact: track the loop index (or a running prefix pointer into the swap trace) at the moment `best` is updated in both polish() and polishConstrained(), and expose it (e.g. `PolishResult.bestAtIter` or by truncating the trace itself to that point before returning it). This is cheap — it's an integer already implicitly known at `best = g.copy()` — and doing it there avoids a caller having to re-simulate the search or diff two graphs to find where 'the construction of the returned graph' actually ends.
gating.invariant: For the ordered list S of every applied-and-not-reverted swap in polish's loop, there exists an index i (0 <= i <= |S|) such that replaying S[0..i] onto the loop's starting graph yields an edge set identical to PolishResult.graph's; today no field of PolishResult (or the constrainedGreedy.ts equivalent) lets a caller recover i without independently re-deriving it.

Normalize NaN (and any non-finite numeric tag) to `null` in `tagOf`, so an ungroupable value means "no group" instead of silently prohibiting nothing.
confirmed.invariant: For all (n, tags, policy): `Constraints.fromTags` either throws before its first `prohibit()` call, or n is an integer in [0, MAX_CONSTRAINED_N] and the returned `prohibitedCount` is <= a declared pair cap. Equivalently: the number of loop iterations and Set insertions performed by `fromTags` is bounded by a constant independent of the caller's `n`, for every input on which it does not throw.

confirmed.theme: The tag-policy switch that lib/CLAUDE.md names as the core's genuine open/closed seam has never been exercised by a real caller, so its 'this seam pays' claim is asserted, not demonstrated
confirmed.summary: TagPolicy (line 46) is a union of exactly one string literal ("prohibit_same"), and Constraints.fromTags's switch (lines 114-126) has exactly one case plus a default throw. I added a second case ("require_same", compiling same-tag groups to required rather than prohibited pairs) as a trial extension: it required touching only this one switch and the TagPolicy union — no other file in lib/src or app/ references TagPolicy or calls fromTags outside lib/test/constrained.test.ts (grep across the whole repo confirms zero non-test callers). Structurally the switch is trivial to extend, which is real evidence for the CLAUDE.md claim; but because fromTags itself has no live caller anywhere in app/ (confirmed by grep, and independently noted in lib/CLAUDE.md's own 'fromTags has no caller outside lib/test' line about a different defect), the seam's payoff is currently untested by any real usage pattern, and a second policy has no product requirement to satisfy today (PROJECT_PLAN.md F7 only ever names prohibit_same for households/teams/shifts).
confirmed.failure: Not a functional failure — a documentation/confidence gap: reviewers and future contributors are told 'add a case, don't edit callers' as a proven property of this codebase, but no caller has ever forced that path to prove itself, and TagPolicy's single-literal union type provides no compiler pressure to add anything either.
confirmed.invariant: caseOnly — no behavioural invariant is violated; the observation is that grep for 'fromTags(' outside lib/test/ and lib/src/ returns zero matches, which is mechanically checkable but does not gate correctness.
confirmed.remediation: No action needed now. When F7's tag UI actually lands and fromTags gets a real caller, re-verify the OCP claim against whatever second policy first ships (if any) rather than assuming today's structural ease transfers unchanged once fromTags carries the hardening lib/CLAUDE.md already flags as owed at that point (n-guard, dominant-tag O(n²) cap, NaN handling).

confirmed.theme: Both swap-polish passes return a mid-search energy-best snapshot, not the terminal state of their own accepted-swap trajectory, and nothing in their public result exposes where the two diverge — which is exactly the gap the project's own next roadmap item (F11 construction replay) will hit if it instruments these loops the obvious way
confirmed.summary: PROJECT_PLAN.md's F11 entry states plainly that replay needs a construction trace and that this is core work, not UI-only, because Graph.edgeList() only returns a canonical sort. I traced what the natural fix looks like: ringGreedy's for(;;) loop (greedy.ts:171-185) and repairDegrees's pass loop (greedy.ts:265-314) each add edges in a genuine causal order that a trace can record cheaply (O(1) per edge, off the O(n²) hot inner loops) and that order IS the graph returned. polish.ts's loop is different in kind: `g` (the live mutating graph, polish.ts:115-150) keeps advancing after `best` is last updated — Metropolis accepts non-improving moves (line 131) that mutate `g` but never touch `best` — so the loop can run thousands of further accepted-and-kept swaps on `g` after the swap that produced the returned `best` (polish.ts:136-140, `best = g.copy()`). The function returns `best`, not `g`. `PolishResult`'s fields are exactly `{ graph, aspl, connected, iters }` (polish.ts:40-45) — `iters` is the total loop count that ran, not the index at which `best` was captured. `polishConstrained` in constrainedGreedy.ts has the identical shape (constrainedGreedy.ts:220-228, `best = g.copy()` on `next.energy < bestEnergy`), and its return type carries no run-level metrics at all (module comment at constrainedGreedy.ts:139-141 explicitly says so). A naive implementation of F11's trace — record every applied (non-reverted) swap in loop order and replay it start-to-finish — reconstructs the fully-mutated final `g`, which is NOT the graph either function actually returns to its caller.
confirmed.failure: Recording swap trace S (every applied, non-reverted swap in polish's loop, in order) and replaying all of S against the input graph produces a graph edge-set-identical to the loop's final `g`, which for a typical anneal run (Metropolis accepts moves worse than best) differs from PolishResult.graph (the returned `best`). Concretely: with mode:'anneal' and enough iterations after the last improving accept, `S` replayed in full will diverge from `res.graph`'s edge set, while no field of `res` names the prefix length of `S` that does reconstruct it.
confirmed.remediation: Before instrumenting these loops for F11, add the missing correspondence explicitly rather than reconstructing it after the fact: track the loop index (or a running prefix pointer into the swap trace) at the moment `best` is updated in both polish() and polishConstrained(), and expose it (e.g. `PolishResult.bestAtIter` or by truncating the trace itself to that point before returning it). This is cheap — it's an integer already implicitly known at `best = g.copy()` — and doing it there avoids a caller having to re-simulate the search or diff two graphs to find where 'the construction of the returned graph' actually ends.
confirmed.invariant: For the ordered list S of every applied-and-not-reverted swap in polish's loop, there exists an index i (0 <= i <= |S|) such that replaying S[0..i] onto the loop's starting graph yields an edge set identical to PolishResult.graph's; today no field of PolishResult (or the constrainedGreedy.ts equivalent) lets a caller recover i without independently re-deriving it.

confirmed.theme: Documentation states both buddies and edges fields are empty when build fails, but only edges is actually empty; buddies is an array of n empty arrays, creating false expectations
confirmed.summary: Comment falsely claims buddies field is empty when input is refused; it is actually an n-length array of empty arrays, not empty
confirmed.failure: buildConstrainedBuddyGraph(11, 4, new Constraints(11)) when refused returns result.buddies as [[], [], ...] (length 11), not []; comment claims it should be empty like edges
confirmed.remediation: Change lines 285-286 comment from 'buddies/edges are empty' to 'edges is empty and each person's buddy list is empty (buddies contains n empty arrays)' or similar. Alternatively: provide truly empty buddies array when refused (breaking change for callers checking .length)
confirmed.invariant: When result.report.refusals.length > 0, result.edges must be [] (confirmed) AND result.buddies must either be [] OR contain n empty arrays; documentation must match implementation

confirmed.theme: Comment equates three different option handling strategies as equivalent, obscuring actual implementation differences that a maintainer must understand
confirmed.summary: Comment misleadingly claims polishIters, minSeparation, and priorWeight are all handled identically as 'ignored, not fatal', but they are handled differently
confirmed.failure: polishIters uses boundedPolishIterations which clamps/normalizes via logic; minSeparation passes through to constrainedGreedy which explicitly ignores it with no validation; priorWeight is normalized to 0 here before passing. Comment falsely suggests identical treatment
confirmed.remediation: Replace lines 370-371 with accurate comment naming the actual behaviors: 'this entry point normalises bad input (consistent with how polishIters falls back to default and how minSeparation is ignored), so it never throws'
confirmed.invariant: Each option (polishIters, minSeparation, priorWeight) must have a clear documented behavior in code comments that accurately reflects how it is actually validated/normalized/ignored; no two should be grouped as equivalent unless their handling is actually identical

deferrals.theme: an attacker-chosen size drives unbounded work before any gate can refuse it
deferrals.summary: `Constraints.fromTags` is the only entry point in the core that takes a roster size on faith. `degreeOf` in the same file, the `Graph` constructor, `validate`, `ringGreedy` and `constrainedGreedy` all guard `n` first; `fromTags` runs `for (let i = 0; i < n; i++)` with no validation and inserts one Set key per same-tag pair, so both the loop trip count and the O(n^2) materialization are paid inside the constructor — `validate`'s MAX_CONSTRAINED_N refusal only ever sees the result. This is the documented deferral in lib/CLAUDE.md; I re-verified it still reproduces and re-verified the no-caller condition it rests on (grep across app/src and lib/src finds references only in lib/test), so it stays a deferral rather than becoming gating.
deferrals.failure: Measured against the built dist: `Constraints.fromTags(1e9, [])` spins a bare 1e9-iteration loop for 2.8 s and returns — linear in an unvalidated argument, so 1e15 is ~46 days and there is no gate anywhere on the path. `Constraints.fromTags(20000, new Array(20000).fill('A'))` runs 17.1 s and then dies with `RangeError: Set maximum size exceeded` — an uncatchable-by-design failure that happens strictly before any caller could invoke `validate`, which would have refused n=20000 against MAX_CONSTRAINED_N in microseconds. `fromTags(3000, Array(3000).fill('A'))` builds 4,498,500 keys in 4.0 s. Separately, `fromTags(4, [NaN,NaN,NaN,NaN])` yields prohibitedCount 0 because NaN !== NaN, silently inverting the `prohibit_same` policy for a numeric tag column.
deferrals.remediation: Guard `n` as the first statement, with the same predicate the rest of the module uses (`Number.isInteger(n) && n >= 0 && n <= MAX_CONSTRAINED_N`), and throw the module's own message rather than letting the loop run. Then pre-count group sizes in one O(n) pass and refuse against an explicit pair cap BEFORE entering the double loop, so the cost is decided from the counts and never from the insertions. Normalize NaN (and any non-finite numeric tag) to `null` in `tagOf`, so an ungroupable value means "no group" instead of silently prohibiting nothing.
deferrals.invariant: For all (n, tags, policy): `Constraints.fromTags` either throws before its first `prohibit()` call, or n is an integer in [0, MAX_CONSTRAINED_N] and the returned `prohibitedCount` is <= a declared pair cap. Equivalently: the number of loop iterations and Set insertions performed by `fromTags` is bounded by a constant independent of the caller's `n`, for every input on which it does not throw.
